title: Ben Johnson Stays Non‑Committal on Week 4 Starting Quarterback, NBC Sports Reports
body:
The Chicago Bears entered the final week of preseason with a lingering question that could shape their 2024 campaign: who will take the snaps under center in Week 4? Head coach Ben Johnson offered no definitive answer, telling reporters, “We’ll see how it plays out all week,” when pressed about the quarterback hierarchy. The coy response underscores a broader uncertainty at the position, as the Bears juggle a crowded roster, lingering injuries and a desire to evaluate talent without compromising competitive balance.

The Bears arrived at the preseason finale with three quarterbacks vying for the starting role: veteran starter Justin Fields, who has shown flashes of brilliance but also struggled with consistency; second‑year backup J.J. McCarthy, whose poise in limited action has drawn praise; and newly signed free‑agent Nathaniel “Nate” Davis, a former backup who earned a roster spot after a strong showing in training camp. Each brings a different skill set: Fields’ dual‑threat ability, McCarthy’s accuracy and poise in the pocket, and Davis’ experience as a game manager. Johnson’s non‑committal stance suggests he is using the remaining preseason games to assess not just raw performance but also how each quarterback adapts to the evolving playbook and the chemistry with a revamped offensive line.

The decision carries weight beyond the immediate roster. Chicago’s offense has been a focal point of criticism in recent seasons, with the unit ranking near the bottom of the league in both passing yards and points per game. A clear starter could provide the stability needed for a cohesive offensive identity, while a rotating approach might keep defenses guessing but risk stalling the development of any single quarterback. Moreover, the Bears’ front office has signaled a willingness to invest in the position, having allocated significant cap space to retain Fields and to bring in veteran depth. If Johnson ultimately leans toward Fields, the team may be signaling confidence in his long‑term potential, despite the pressure to deliver immediate results. Conversely, a surprise promotion of McCarthy or Davis could indicate a strategic pivot toward a more conservative, perhaps more reliable, offensive scheme.

The timing of the decision also intersects with the Bears’ broader roster construction. The offensive line, still retooling after a slew of injuries, will be tested in the upcoming regular‑season matchups, particularly against divisional rivals with formidable pass rushes. A quarterback who can extend plays with his legs may alleviate pressure, but could also expose the line to additional wear. On the other hand, a pocket passer who relies on quick releases and precise timing routes could reduce sack totals but demands a higher level of protection. Johnson’s comment that the situation will “play out all week” hints at an intention to monitor not only the quarterbacks’ individual performances but also how the line and skill positions respond under different leadership.

Analysts have pointed out that the Bears’ preseason schedule offers limited opportunities to gauge true quarterback aptitude. With only a handful of snaps against second‑string defenses, the sample size is small, and the intensity is not reflective of regular‑season pressure. Yet, the coaching staff can glean valuable insights from practice reps, film study and the quarterbacks’ ability to command the huddle. The Bears’ offensive coordinator, Mike Kafka, has emphasized a “next‑man‑up” philosophy throughout camp, encouraging competition and rewarding execution. This approach aligns with Johnson’s public stance, allowing the decision to remain fluid until the final week of preparation.

Looking ahead, the Bears’ quarterback decision will likely crystallize in the days leading up to the regular‑season opener. If Fields solidifies his role, Chicago can focus on tailoring its offensive scheme to his athleticism, potentially revitalizing a stagnant attack. Should McCarthy or Davis earn the nod, the team may prioritize a more methodical, ball‑control strategy aimed at minimizing turnovers and protecting a still‑developing defense. Regardless of the outcome, Johnson’s measured response underscores a commitment to thorough evaluation, a process that could set the tone for a franchise eager to break out of its recent mediocrity. The upcoming weeks will reveal whether the Bears can translate preseason intrigue into a decisive, confidence‑building move at the most pivotal position on the field.
